node.label: W. E. B. Du Bois
node.description: Historian and social investigator whose selected works move between documentary history, an urban survey and the form of the essay. The 1896 slave-trade monograph begins from laws and official records while acknowledging weak economic evidence. The Souls of Black Folk (1903) articulates double consciousness. Chad Williams reads Black Reconstruction (1935) as a history of Black political agency and defeated multiracial democracy; Elijah Anderson rereads the Philadelphia survey as an account of racial exclusion. Hartman’s later criticism of the survey’s class and gender judgments is recorded as a distinct disagreement.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Suppression of the African Slave-Trade (1896); The Philadelphia Negro (1899; Isabel Eaton’s domestic-service investigation separately credited); The Souls of Black Folk (1903); Black Reconstruction (1935). Readers: Chad Williams (online 2022, print 2023), Elijah Anderson (2023), Saidiya Hartman (2020).
node.date_label: The Suppression of the African Slave-Trade (1896) · The Philadelphia Negro (1899) · The Souls of Black Folk (1903) · Black Reconstruction (1935)
node.scope_note: Read in part: the 1896 preface and chapter I opening, and the 1903 Forethought and chapter I, in public-domain transcriptions. The 1899 and 1935 books are known here through the named readings by Anderson and Williams. Their conclusions are attributed to them. Hartman’s criticism comes from her 2020 interview, not a newly read passage of Wayward Lives. Period racial/evolutionary vocabulary is historical evidence, not endorsed terminology. Later activism and writings are not comprehensively surveyed. Existing edge_241 retains its Du Bois/Gilroy diaspora-resource claim; no duplicate personal Atlantic arrow is added.

proposed_edges.relationship: Black Reconstruction (1935) reinterprets emancipation and Reconstruction through Black agency and an interrupted experiment in multiracial democracy, as Chad Williams reads it (2022).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Williams’s introduction, read, supplies this characterization; the full 1935 book is not newly read. The existing field roster is retained, and this contribution does not claim sole founding of Black historical scholarship.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Philadelphia Negro (1899) examines a specific Black urban community; Elijah Anderson’s 2023 introduction emphasizes employment discrimination and the limits of expecting reform from informed employers.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: A named reader’s interpretation of the 1899 Philadelphia survey. This is a contribution through one study, not a claim that Du Bois founded all urban history. Isabel Eaton’s domestic-service study is separately credited; it is not treated as Du Bois’s sole-authored research.

verification.note: Publisher-authorized introduction excerpt read in full. Anderson interprets Du Bois’s 1899 social survey through racial exclusion in employment and its contemporary relevance. new_sources.citation: Chad Williams, “In the Shadow of World War: Revisiting W. E. B. Du Bois’s Black Reconstruction,” Du Bois Review 20:1 (2023), 43–55; first online 11 July 2022.

verification.note: Open-access abstract, introduction and opening World War I section read on Cambridge Core. Williams characterizes the 1935 reinterpretation of Reconstruction as multiracial democracy defeated and relates its writing to Du Bois’s wartime political development. Black Reconstruction itself remains unread in this pass. Online 2022 and print-issue 2023 dates are distinguished.
